lessons.title: Index laws
lessons.summary: Use positive, zero and negative indices, including powers with the same base.
lessons.objective: Use positive, zero and negative indices, including powers with the same base.
lessons.before: Write a small power as repeated multiplication before using the shortcut.
lessons.ideas:
When the bases match, a product joins the factor lists. Add the indices.

Subtract the denominator's index from the numerator's index. A negative result leaves factors underneath.

For non-zero \(a\), \(a^0=1\) and \(a^{-n}=\frac{1}{a^n}\).
lessons.method:
Show the step that explains your answer.

Show the step that explains your answer.

Show the step that explains your answer.
mistakes: Multiplying the indices counts the wrong number of factors.
Swapping the order of subtraction reverses the fraction.
A negative index does not make a positive base negative.

examples.title: Count the factors
examples.question:
\(5^{2} \times 5^{1}\) is written as \(5^n\).

  1. Find \(n\).

    [2]

  2. Explain whether the same shortcut applies to \(5^{2}\times 6^{1}\).

    [1]
examples.solution:
(a) Multiplication joins two strings of equal factors. Add their lengths.

\(2+1=3\).

\(3\)

(b) The factors in the two powers are different.

The bases differ, so a single-base product rule does not apply.

examples.title: Cancel matching powers
examples.question:
Divide \(6^{3}\) by \(6^{4}\).

  1. Write the result as \(6^n\). Find \(n\).

    [2]

  2. Give the result as a fraction.

    [1]
examples.solution:
(a) \(3-(4)=-1\). There are more base factors in the denominator.

\(-1\)

(b) \(6^{-1}=1/6^{1}\).

\(\frac{1}{6}\)

examples.title: Zero and negative powers
examples.question:
You compare \(7^{-1}\) and \(7^0\).

  1. Evaluate \(7^{-1}\).

    [2]

  2. Explain why the other value is 1.

    [1]
examples.solution:
(a) A negative index means take the reciprocal of the positive power.

\(\frac{1}{7}\)

(b) A non-zero number divided by itself is 1.

\(7^{5}/7^{5}=7^0=1\)

lessons.title: Powers of ten and standard form
lessons.summary: Scale numbers by powers of ten and describe very large or very small numbers in standard form.
lessons.objective: Scale numbers by powers of ten and describe very large or very small numbers in standard form.
lessons.before: Use the value of each place, rather than imagining a loose decimal point.
lessons.ideas:
Every place to the left is ten times the previous place. Scaling by ten repeatedly follows the index.

Standard form is \(A imes10^n\) with \(1\leq A<10\) and integer \(n\).

Dividing by one hundredth multiplies by 100. Check whether your result should grow or shrink.
lessons.method:
Show the step that explains your answer.

Show the step that explains your answer.

Show the step that explains your answer.
mistakes: Going in the wrong direction makes a number smaller when it should get bigger.
A coefficient of 12.3 must be changed along with its power of ten.
Dividing by a number less than 1 can make a positive value larger.

examples.title: Shift the place values
examples.question:
The measurement display starts at \(0.034\).

  1. Find the new reading after multiplying by \(10^2\).

    [2]

  2. Describe how to return to the starting value.

    [1]
examples.solution:
(a) Multiplying by \(10^2\) makes every place worth 100 times as much.

\(\frac{17}{5}\)

(b) Use the inverse operation.

Divide by \(10^2\).

examples.title: Use standard form
examples.question:
A microscope display gives the number \(0.00125\). In standard form it is \(A\times10^n\).

  1. Find \(n\).

    [2]

  2. State \(A\).

    [1]
examples.solution:
(a) The coefficient is \(\frac{5}{4}\). The original number is \(10^{-3}\) times as large as this coefficient.

\(-3\)

(b) Move the decimal point so exactly one non-zero digit lies before it.

\(\frac{5}{4}\)

examples.title: Divide by a negative power of ten
examples.question:
A counter reads \(2.16\).

  1. Evaluate \(2.16\div10^{-5}\).

    [2]

  2. Give the equivalent operation using a positive index.

    [1]
examples.solution:
(a) \(10^{-5}=1/10^5\). Dividing by that fraction multiplies by its reciprocal.

\(216000\)

(b) Take the reciprocal of the divisor.

\(2.16\times10^5\)

lessons.title: Number types and estimated roots
lessons.summary: Distinguish rational and irrational numbers and estimate square and cube roots.
lessons.objective: Distinguish rational and irrational numbers and estimate square and cube roots.
lessons.before: Try to write the number as one integer divided by another non-zero integer.
lessons.ideas:
A terminating or recurring decimal is rational. A square root of a positive non-square integer is irrational.

The square root lies between their positive roots. Compare squares before using a calculator.

Compare the volume to nearby perfect cubes. Their edges give lower and upper estimates.
lessons.method:
Show the step that explains your answer.

Show the step that explains your answer.

Show the step that explains your answer.
mistakes: A radical written with a root sign can still be rational if it simplifies to an integer.
The side length of a square is the square root of its area.
A cube has three dimensions. Use cubes rather than squares.

examples.title: Classify the number
examples.question:
Compare \(\sqrt{38}\), \(\sqrt{36}\), \(3\) and \(0.06\).

  1. Which one is irrational? Options: A. \(sqrt{36}\). B. \(3\). C. \(0.06\). D. \(sqrt{38}\).

    [2]

  2. Explain why the ordinary decimal is rational.

    [1]
examples.solution:
(a) 38 is not a perfect square. Its square root cannot be written as a ratio of integers.

\(sqrt{38}\)

(b) A terminating decimal equals an integer divided by a power of ten.

\(0.06=\frac{6}{100}\)

examples.title: Trap a square root
examples.question:
A square tile has area 19 square units.

  1. Give the whole number just below its side length.

    [2]

  2. State the next whole number above the length.

    [1]
examples.solution:
(a) \(16<19<25\). Take the square root of all three numbers.

\(4\)

(b) Use the bigger of the two square numbers.

\(5\)

examples.title: Trap a cube root
examples.question:
A cube holds 1336 cubic units.

  1. Give the whole number just below its edge length.

    [2]

  2. Write an inequality for its exact edge length.

    [1]
examples.solution:
(a) \(1331<1336<1728\). Take cube roots.

\(11\)

(b) Neither cube equals the given volume.

\(11

questions.title: Classify the number
questions.prompt_html:
Compare \(\sqrt{56}\), \(\sqrt{49}\), \(1\) and \(0.07\).

  1. Which one is irrational? Options: A. \(0.07\). B. \(sqrt{56}\). C. \(sqrt{49}\). D. \(1\).

    [2]

  2. Explain why the ordinary decimal is rational.

    [1]
questions.solution_html:
(a) 56 is not a perfect square. Its square root cannot be written as a ratio of integers.

\(sqrt{56}\)

(b) A terminating decimal equals an integer divided by a power of ten.

\(0.07=\frac{7}{100}\)
questions.hint_html: Check which square root lies between consecutive integers.
